draft.title: Comparing religious and non-religious worldviews
card: Meaning
Many religious worldviews find meaning in a relationship with God or a sacred order. Many non-religious worldviews find meaning in human relationships, work, learning and personal goals.
Ethics
Many religious traditions ground ethics in sacred texts, teachings or the will of God. Many non-religious worldviews ground ethics in human reason, empathy and shared social values.
Life after death
Many religious worldviews teach some form of life after death, such as heaven or rebirth. Many non-religious worldviews hold that death is the end of a person's existence.
Worldviews can still share values, such as care for others, fairness and honesty, even when they give different reasons for them.
draft.remember: Worldviews can differ on meaning, ethics and death, yet still share values.

a.q: Which statement best describes how many religious and non-religious worldviews can relate on ethics?
opts: They can share values but give different reasons for them
Different reasons mean they must hold different values
They share both the same values and the same reasons
They share reasons but they differ on what is valued
a.why: The card says worldviews can share values such as care for others while grounding them differently, for example in sacred teachings or in human reason. The tempting option that different reasons mean different values is wrong, because shared values can have different foundations.
a.clue: Think about values and the reasons behind them as two separate things.

b.q: Priya follows a religion and Tom is a humanist. Both volunteer at a food bank because they believe in caring for people in need. What does this show?
opts: Different worldviews can share a value like care for others
Their worldviews must agree on the source of ethics
Their worldviews must agree on life after death
Only a religious worldview can motivate care for others
b.why: Both act on the shared value of care for others, though Priya may ground it in her tradition's teachings and Tom in human reason and empathy. Agreeing on a value does not mean agreeing on its basis or on other questions, so the second option is wrong.
b.clue: Shared actions do not mean shared reasons.

a.best: They can share values but give different reasons for them

b.best: Different worldviews can share a value like care for others

a.q: A Christian and a humanist both believe honesty matters. How do their views on honesty most likely compare?
opts: Same value, different grounds for holding it
Same value, same grounds for holding it
Different values, same grounds for holding them
Different values, different grounds for holding them
a.why: Both hold honesty as a value, but the Christian is likely to ground it in sacred teachings and the humanist in human reason and empathy. The tempting option of the same value on the same grounds is wrong, because the two worldviews draw their ethics from different sources.
a.clue: Separate the value itself from the reason for holding it.

b.q: Priya follows a religion and Tom is a humanist. Both volunteer at a food bank because they believe in caring for people in need. What does this example show?
opts: People with different worldviews share some values
People who share a value share its source of ethics
People who share a value agree on life after death
Caring for others is a sign of religious belief
b.why: Both act on the shared value of care for others, though Priya may ground it in her tradition's teachings and Tom in human reason and empathy. The idea that sharing a value means sharing its source of ethics is wrong, because the same value can rest on different foundations.
b.clue: Shared actions do not mean shared reasons.
